Angola.summary: Most of the later population descends from farming cultures that appeared c. 1000-500 BCE and were working iron by the first centuries CE. Archaeology from this region is very scarce, so little can be said specifically about c. 570-632. The Kongo and Ndongo kingdoms lay centuries in the future.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities occupy the region; almost no sites from this period have been dated.

sources.title: History of Angola
Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)

Benin.summary: Iron-using farming communities lived in this part of West Africa during the first millennium CE, but archaeological evidence for the period is very limited. The later kingdoms of Allada and Dahomey were many centuries away.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities occupy the region; almost no sites from this era are published.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Botswana.polity: Foragers and herders; early iron-using farmers at Tsodilo
Botswana.summary: In the north-west, foraging dominated the Tsodilo Hills until about 600 CE; the Iron Age village of Divuyu there dates to roughly the 6th-8th centuries, with iron and copper working. The Toutswe farming tradition of the east began only around 700. No written records exist.

events.t: Divuyu at Tsodilo Hills is occupied by iron- and copper-working farmers, dated broadly to the 6th-8th centuries.

sources.title: Tsodilo (nomination file / ICOMOS documentation, No. 1021)
Iron age metal working at the Tsodilo Hills, Northwestern Botswana
Mookodi, article on Toutswe-tradition settlement, Pula: Botswana Journal of African Studies

Burkina Faso.summary: Iron production in the region was very old: Douroula, part of a UNESCO World Heritage property, dates back to the 8th century BCE. The property's other furnace sites show intensified production in the second millennium CE. Little is specifically dated to c. 570-632, and no written records survive.

events.t: Iron smelting, attested at Douroula since the 8th century BCE, is long established; specific sites of this era are poorly dated.

sources.title: Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy Sites of Burkina Faso

Burundi.polity: Iron-using farmers and forest foragers of the Great Lakes
Burundi.summary: Highland farmers here belonged to the Early Iron Age Urewe tradition of the Great Lakes region, where iron smelting began in the first millennium BCE. Forest foragers lived alongside them. The later kingdom of Burundi did not yet exist. Archaeology gives only a general picture.

events.t: Iron-using highland farming communities continue the long Great Lakes iron tradition; few sites are dated to this era.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)

Cameroon.polity: Farming and foraging communities; Lake Chad plain settlements in the north
Cameroon.summary: The Cameroon-Nigeria borderlands are the likely homeland of the Bantu languages. In southern Cameroon, radiocarbon evidence shows a sharp population collapse c. 400-600 CE and low activity for centuries after. In the far north, settlement mounds of the Lake Chad plain were occupied. Archaeology is the only evidence.

events.t: Southern Cameroon's forest communities are much reduced after a population collapse c. 400-600 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
sources.publisher: Science Advances (AAAS), open access via PubMed Central

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)
Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Central African Rep..summary: Very little archaeology from this period has been dated in this region. To the south, studies of the wider Congo rainforest show a widespread population collapse between c. 400 and 600 CE. The megaliths near Bouar are of uncertain date and cannot be securely placed in this period. No written sources exist.

events.t: In the wider Congo rainforest to the south, human activity is very low after a collapse c. 400-600 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
sources.publisher: Science Advances (AAAS), open access via PubMed Central

Congo.summary: Iron-using Bantu-speaking communities had spread along the Congo's tributaries in earlier centuries, but radiocarbon evidence shows a widespread population collapse across the Congo rainforest c. 400-600 CE, strongest in the Lower Congo, with low activity until resettlement around 1000. The Kongo and Tio kingdoms came much later.

events.t: After a rainforest-wide population collapse c. 400-600 CE, human activity remains low; recovery comes around 1000 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
sources.publisher: Science Advances (AAAS), open access via PubMed Central

sources.title: Central Africa: The Iron Age

Côte d'Ivoire.summary: Iron-using farming communities lived in the West African forest and savanna zones in the first millennium CE, but very few sites in this country have been excavated for this period. The Akan and other later states had not yet formed.

events.t: Iron-using farmers occupy savanna and forest zones; few sites from this era have been excavated.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Dem. Rep. Congo.polity: Farming and foraging communities; Kamilambian iron-users in the Upemba
Dem. Rep. Congo.summary: Across the Congo rainforest, including the inner basin, radiocarbon evidence shows a population collapse c. 400-600 CE and low activity until c. 1000. In the Upemba Depression in the south-east, the Kamilambian, the area's earliest ironworking culture (c. 6th-8th century), preceded the Kisalian, which began c. mid-8th century.

events.t: Kamilambian communities, the Upemba Depression's earliest ironworking culture (c. 6th-8th century), occupy sites such as Kamilamba and Sanga.

sources.title: Nicolas Nikis, Upemba Depression (The Encyclopedia of Ancient History, 2021)
sources.publisher: Wiley-Blackwell; author copy via Royal Museum for Central Africa

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
sources.publisher: Science Advances (AAAS), open access via PubMed Central

Eq. Guinea.summary: The mainland lies within the Congo rainforest, where radiocarbon studies covering neighbouring southern Cameroon and Gabon show a sharp population collapse c. 400-600 CE and low activity for centuries afterwards. The early history of Bioko island in this period is poorly known.

events.t: Rainforest communities in the region are much reduced after a population collapse c. 400-600 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
sources.publisher: Science Advances (AAAS), open access via PubMed Central

Gabon.summary: Iron smelting had reached Central Africa's western forest long before, but radiocarbon evidence shows a sharp population collapse in Gabon c. 400-600 CE, with very low human activity until a new expansion phase from c. 1000 CE. No written sources exist.

events.t: Gabon's forest is thinly occupied after a population collapse c. 400-600 CE; resettlement follows from c. 1000.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
sources.publisher: Science Advances (AAAS), open access via PubMed Central

sources.title: Central Africa: The Iron Age

Gambia.polity: Communities of the Senegambian megalithic zone
Gambia.summary: Along the Gambia River, communities raised circles of laterite pillars, quarried with iron tools, beside burial mounds, as at Wassu and Kerbatch. Excavated material from the sites suggests dates from the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE. Nothing is known of their rulers or languages from writing.

events.t: The Senegambian stone-circle tradition, spanning the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE, is in use at sites such as Wassu.

sources.title: Stone Circles of Senegambia

Ghana.polity: Farming communities (not the medieval Ghana empire)
Ghana.summary: Modern Ghana lies far from the medieval Ghana (Wagadu) empire, which was in the western Sahel. Iron-using farmers lived in the savanna and forest, but sites of this period are few. The Koma Land terracotta mounds of the north are dated mainly to later centuries (c. 13th-19th) in published research.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities occupy savanna and forest; few sites from this era are dated.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)
Kankpeyeng & Nkumbaan, Ancient Shrines? New Insights on the Komaland Sites of Northern Ghana

Guinea.summary: Iron-using farming communities lived in the upland savanna and forest zones of West Africa in this era. The great states of the region came centuries later. The period is known only through very limited archaeology.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities occupy the highlands and upper Niger; few sites are dated to this era.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Guinea-Bissau.polity: Coastal farming and fishing communities (poorly documented)
Guinea-Bissau.summary: The coastal estuaries were home to farming and fishing communities, but no written record and very little archaeology survives for this period, so details of their life c. 570-632 are unknown.

events.t: Coastal communities farm and fish; little archaeology exists for the period.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Lesotho.summary: The mountains were home to San hunter-gatherers, the makers of much of the rock art of southern Africa, including Lesotho. Iron Age farming communities settled the area only in later centuries. Evidence is archaeological and rock art.

events.t: San hunter-gatherers occupy mountain rock shelters; farming communities have not yet settled the area.

sources.title: Rock art
David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)

Liberia.polity: Forest farming and foraging communities (poorly documented)
Liberia.summary: Dense rainforest supported small farming and foraging communities. Archaeological research for this era is very limited, so little can be said with confidence.

events.t: Small forest communities farm and forage; the period is almost undocumented archaeologically.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Malawi.polity: Early Iron Age farmers (Nkope tradition) and BaTwa foragers
Malawi.summary: Bantu-speaking farmers making Nkope-tradition pottery lived around Lake Malawi, and ironworking and slash-and-burn cultivation spread in the centuries to about 1200 CE. BaTwa hunter-gatherers, present since the late Stone Age, painted rock shelters such as those at Chongoni. The Chewa states came much later.

events.t: Nkope-tradition Early Iron Age farming villages occupy the Lake Malawi region; BaTwa foragers live alongside them.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)
History of Malawi
Chongoni Rock-Art Area

Namibia.summary: The desert and dry savanna were home to San hunter-gatherers and herders of sheep and some cattle, part of an enduring pastoralist presence in the western half of southern Africa. Much of Namibia's rock art was made by San peoples. Metal-working sites are known but poorly classified. Evidence is archaeological.

events.t: Foragers and herders occupy the region; rock art traditions continue.

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)
Rock art

Nigeria.polity: Iron-using farming communities; Nok culture long ended
Nigeria.summary: The Nok terracotta culture had ended centuries earlier, and the bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu belong to the 9th-10th centuries, so neither fits this period. Iron-using farming villages occupied forest and savanna. Daima near Lake Chad shows a long-lived mound settlement. Ile-Ife's urban growth came later.

events.t: Iron-using communities live at the Daima settlement mound near Lake Chad, occupied over many centuries.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Rwanda.polity: Iron-using farmers and forest foragers of the Great Lakes
Rwanda.summary: Hill farmers belonged to the Urewe tradition of the Great Lakes region, where iron smelting had begun in the first millennium BCE. Forest foragers lived alongside them. The later kingdom of Rwanda was centuries away. Knowledge comes from archaeology.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities continue the long Great Lakes iron tradition; few sites are dated to this era.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)

Senegal.polity: Communities of the Senegambian megalithic zone
Senegal.summary: Communities in the Gambia river region raised circles of laterite pillars, quarried with iron tools, beside burial mounds, as at Sine Ngayene and Wanar. Excavated material suggests dates from the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE. Takrur appears in written sources only centuries later.

events.t: The Senegambian stone-circle tradition is in use at sites such as Sine Ngayene and Wanar.

sources.title: Stone Circles of Senegambia
Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Sierra Leone.polity: Forest and coastal farming and foraging communities (poorly documented)
Sierra Leone.summary: Small farming and foraging communities lived in the forests and along the coast. Very little archaeology has been dated to this period, and no written sources exist.

events.t: Forest and coastal communities farm and forage; few sites are dated to this era.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

South Africa.polity: Iron-using farmers in the east; San foragers and Khoe herders
South Africa.summary: Iron-using farmers, ancestors of today's Bantu-speaking majority, had settled the eastern river valleys and coastal plain from c. 200 CE, keeping cattle and sheep. The Lydenburg Heads from Mpumalanga, the earliest sculpture known from southern Africa, date to c. 500-700 CE. Foragers and herders held the west. Mapungubwe came later.

events.t: The Lydenburg Heads are made by farming communities in Mpumalanga, dated to c. 500-700 CE.

sources.title: South Africa: The Iron Age
Lydenburg heads
sources.publisher: University of Cape Town, Faculty of Humanities

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)

Togo.summary: Farming communities lived in the coastal plains and northern hills. In the Bassar region of the north, iron smelting began in the Early Iron Age, and production grew into a major regional industry in the later Iron Age. Written sources do not exist, and much of the period is undated.

events.t: Bassar communities continue an iron-working tradition begun in the Early Iron Age; large-scale production comes later.

sources.title: de Barros et al., The Early Iron Metallurgy of Bassar, Togo (Azania 55, 2020)

Uganda.polity: Iron-using farmers of the Great Lakes
Uganda.summary: Around Lake Victoria, farmers had used iron and made Urewe-tradition pottery for centuries. Larger centres such as Ntusi developed only after about 1000 CE. No written sources exist, and few sites are dated precisely to this era.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities, heirs of the Urewe tradition, occupy the Lake Victoria basin.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)
Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Zambia.polity: Early Iron Age farmers and foragers
Zambia.summary: Ironworking in central and western Zambia dates to the first five or six centuries CE. Early Iron Age farming villages with distinctive pottery traditions occupied the plateau and valleys, and Kalambo Falls shows long Iron Age occupation. Foragers persisted in many areas. No written sources exist.

events.t: Early Iron Age farming villages occupy the Zambian plateau and the Kalambo Falls area.

sources.title: History of Zambia
David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)

Zimbabwe.polity: Early Iron Age farmers (Gokomere/Ziwa traditions); San foragers
Zimbabwe.summary: Farmers of the Gokomere and Ziwa Early Iron Age traditions grew crops, kept livestock and worked iron. San foragers, makers of much of the region's rock art, still lived in the land. Great Zimbabwe was built only between the 11th and 15th centuries. Evidence is archaeological.

events.t: Gokomere/Ziwa farming villages occupy the plateau; San foragers live alongside them.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)
Great Zimbabwe
Rock art

eSwatini.polity: Iron-using farmers and San foragers (poorly documented)
eSwatini.summary: Iron-using farmers had settled the eastern lowlands of southern Africa, including neighbouring Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal, from c. 200 CE, while San hunter-gatherers lived in the region. Evidence specific to eSwatini in this period is scanty. The Swazi kingdom formed much later.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities occupy the wider eastern lowlands; San foragers remain in the region.

sources.title: South Africa: The Iron Age
David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)
